cover.headline: A cash-rich subsidiary of a Japanese major, priced for growth it has not delivered
cover.lead: Sumitomo Chemical India sells crop-protection chemicals to Indian farmers through 40,000 dealers: about 71% generic products inherited from Excel Crop Care, and 29% patented molecules from its 75% parent, Sumitomo Chemical of Japan. It has no debt and ₹2,523 cr of cash. But revenue has not grown since FY23, and FY27 is being hit by the weakest monsoon since 2015 and a halving of the parent's own orders. The street values it on **P/E on FY28E earnings (36-45x)**, assuming 13-21% a year of earnings growth; we forecast ~8%. Applying **28x to Sep-28E EPS of ₹13.0** gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with HOLD.** The cross-checks are lower (EV/EBITDA ₹340, DCF ₹232) because a P/E on total profit capitalises the interest on the cash pile at 28x. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: Growth has stalled for three years
arguments.p: Revenue was ₹3,511 cr in FY23 and ₹3,238 cr in FY26; domestic crop-protection sales were lower in FY26 than in FY23 (standalone ₹2,485 cr vs ₹2,607 cr). Management concedes peers have grown faster. H1FY27 revenue fell 1%.

arguments.h: The parent is both the moat and the ceiling
arguments.p: Exclusive Indian rights to Sumitomo Japan's patented molecules give the company its best products (Excalia Max sales +50% in H1FY27). But the parent decides the timing: its Japan orders halved this year because it is over-stocked, it dropped and then restored the animal-nutrition business, it has started charging a royalty, and its semiconductor plans in India sit with the parent, not the listed company.

₹2,523 cr of cash, ~15% of the market value, earns ~7% before tax and management has no plan to return it (payout ~12%). The core business earns ~35% on its own equity; the cash drags group ROE down to 16%.

arguments.h: Valuation: de-rated, but not yet cheap
arguments.p: The stock has fallen 41% from its Aug-2026 high and trades at 29.2x our FY27E earnings, versus a ~42x forward median since 2023. On the street's method and our lower growth, 28x gives only ~8% upside, and the cash-adjusted cross-checks give less.

catalysts: Q3FY27 results (Jan-2027): how bad the rabi season is after El Niño and low reservoirs.
IMD's first monsoon forecast for 2027 (April): the FY28 recovery depends on it.
Delhi High Court on the glyphosate restriction (~11-15% of revenue); final paraquat ban (an opportunity).
Parent decisions: Japan orders normalising, new molecules for India, whether its semiconductor-chemicals project sits in the listed company.
Bhavnagar plant for the parent (Q4FY27); any use of the cash (acquisition or payout).

sections.title: Two businesses under one roof: Excel's generics and Sumitomo's patents

blocks.p: Sumitomo Chemical India (SCIL) is the Indian arm of Sumitomo Chemical, Japan's eighth-largest crop-protection company globally. It was a small distributor of its parent's products until 2016-19, when it bought and merged Excel Crop Care, a listed Indian maker of generic pesticides with its own plants and brands. Today it does two quite different things: it **makes and sells generic products** (glyphosate, chlorpyriphos, profenofos, aluminium phosphide) that compete on price with Indian and Chinese makers (~71% of revenue); and it **sells the parent's patented molecules** under Sumitomo brands (~29%), often formulating them locally. It also exports, distributes household insecticides, and passes through animal-feed additives (methionine) for the parent at a fixed 4-5% margin.

blocks.callout: **Corporate actions since listing:** no bonus, split or buyback; share count unchanged at 49.9 cr. One special dividend (₹5, Feb-2024). The parent has held exactly 75% since FY21, so it cannot buy more without first delisting or diluting others.

sections.title: A ₹31,000 cr market growing 5-6% a year, ruled by the monsoon

blocks.p: India's domestic crop-protection market was about ₹30,800 cr in FY25 and is expected to grow 5-6% a year to FY28 (CRISIL). Indian farmers use far less than most countries (~0.6 kg per hectare vs ~3 kg in the US and ~12.6 kg in Brazil), so there is long-term room, but demand in any one year depends on the monsoon, pest attacks and crop prices. India is also the world's third-largest exporter of these chemicals (~₹38,000 cr in FY25), mainly generics, priced against Chinese supply. The market is fragmented: global innovators (Bayer, Syngenta, BASF, Corteva, Sumitomo), large Indian firms (UPL, PI, Coromandel, Rallis, Dhanuka) and hundreds of small generic makers.

sections.title: The parent: the source of the best products, and of the biggest uncertainty

blocks.p: Sumitomo Chemical (SCC) owns 75% and supplies the molecules that set SCIL apart from Indian generic makers. SCIL has the exclusive right to sell SCC's patented products in India under SCC brands, historically without paying a royalty. India has recently been moved into SCC's first tier of countries for early trials of new molecules (two are in Indian trials before their global launch). SCC also wants India as a manufacturing base: SCIL is building plants at Bhavnagar, Tarapur and Dahej to make molecules for SCC worldwide.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** SCIL has a **distribution moat** (one of the widest dealer networks in Indian agrochemicals, with disciplined credit: receivables 83 days and almost no sales returns) and **privileged access to a global innovator's molecules**. That explains its ~20% EBITDA margin, above Indian generic peers. But it has **no cost advantage** in the 71% of revenue that is generic, and **no research of its own** (0.45% of sales). A distribution business with a borrowed pipeline deserves a premium to generic makers, but not the 40x+ that assumes it can grow at mid-teens: it has not done so since FY23.

sections.title: A monsoon business: two quarters make two-thirds of the profit

blocks.p: Most of India's crops are sown in the kharif (monsoon) season from June to September, and that is when farmers spray most insecticides and herbicides. So April-September (Q1 and Q2) is Sumitomo's peak: in FY26 the first half brought 61% of revenue and 66% of net profit. October-March (rabi, the winter crop) is smaller. One weak monsoon, or one season of excess stock at dealers, can wipe out a year's growth.

pair.title: Quarterly revenue: peaks every June and September quarter
Quarterly net profit

blocks.callout: **The latest season was weak:** Q2FY27 revenue fell 2% and net profit 12% from a year earlier, and H1FY27 revenue was flat (₹1,970 cr vs ₹1,987 cr). H1 net profit still rose 4%, but only because other income almost doubled in Q1, partly from a one-off ₹27 cr insurance claim for a 2023 plant fire. This matters for valuation: the June and September quarters set the tone for the whole year.

sections.title: Revenue has stalled for three years; profit grew on margins and interest income

blocks.p: Sumitomo Chemical India's revenue rose from ₹2,425 cr in FY20 to ₹3,511 cr in FY23, then fell 19% in FY24 as the whole Indian crop-protection industry cut prices and cleared excess stock. It has recovered only to ₹3,238 cr in FY26, so revenue is still 8% below its FY23 peak. Profit has done better: net profit reached a record ₹543 cr in FY26 because the EBITDA margin rose to 20.7% (from 13.8% in FY20) and interest income on a growing cash pile added ₹131 cr.

pair.title: Revenue: flat since FY23
Net profit: a record ₹543 cr in FY26
EBITDA margin: up from 14% to 21%
Other income now ~18% of pre-tax profit

blocks.callout: **Our view:** over FY23-26 revenue fell 3% a year while net profit grew 3% a year. The gap came from a higher margin and treasury income. Both have limits: the margin is already at a record, and interest income grows only as fast as the cash pile. Profit growth from here needs revenue growth.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean audit, but watch interest income, dealer schemes and one-offs

bullets: **Interest income.** Other income was ₹147 cr in FY26, ~20% of pre-tax profit. It grows only as fast as the cash pile and falls when deposit rates fall; it should not be valued like operating profit.

**Dealer rebates and schemes.** Revenue is shown after ₹333 cr of rebates and discounts (9.3% of gross sales). The auditor flags the estimate as a key audit matter. The year-end liability for "additional discounts and schemes" rose 16.5% in FY26 while sales rose 3%.
**Sales returns** were ₹22 cr in FY26 (₹9 cr in FY25) but remain tiny (0.6% of gross sales); management says it has no sales-return policy.
**One-offs.** Q1FY27 profit included a ₹27 cr insurance claim for a 2023 fire at Bhavnagar; Q3FY26 included a ₹16 cr Labour Codes charge.
**Animal-nutrition pass-through** sales (₹185 cr in FY26, up to ₹1,000 cr of purchases approved for FY27) add revenue at a 4-5% margin: they flatter growth and dilute the margin percentage.
**Barrix goodwill** of ₹60 cr sits on a business that made ₹0.08 cr profit in FY26 (impairment test is a key audit matter).
**Data note.** Screener shows an 80% payout for FY25; it belongs to FY24 (₹5 special dividend). FY25's payout was ~12%.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** The audit (B S R & Co., KPMG network, since FY25) is unqualified and the business generates real cash (₹446 cr operating cash flow in FY26). The amber is for the growing dealer-scheme liability and the large share of profit that comes from interest income.

sections.title: No debt, a growing cash pile, and dealer credit as the main use of money

blocks.p: Sumitomo carries almost no debt (₹63 cr, mostly leases). Over FY21-26 it generated ₹2,691 cr of operating cash, spent only ₹414 cr on capex and paid ₹532 cr in dividends (including a ₹5 special dividend in FY24), so cash has piled up: ₹2,113 cr at Mar-2026 and ₹2,523 cr at Sep-2026 on the company's own count, which includes ~₹840 cr of deposits placed with companies and banks that sit under "other assets" in the balance sheet below. The main use of working capital is credit to dealers and stock for the season: receivable days have fallen from 128 in FY20 to 83 in FY26, while inventory days (166) remain high, as is normal in crop protection, where products must be stocked months before the season.

sections.title: Ownership: 75% Japanese parent, and Indian funds buying the rest

blocks.p: Sumitomo Chemical (Japan) owns exactly 75%, the most a listed company's promoter may hold, with nothing pledged. Of the 25% free float, Indian mutual funds have doubled their stake to 7.7% in three years while retail holders shrank from ~149,000 to ~109,000; foreign investors own under 3%.

sections.title: Our forecasts: ~8% earnings growth, well below the street

blocks.p: We forecast revenue as one line, because the company reports one segment and does not give sales or profit by product. FY27 is nearly flat after the weak monsoon and the parent's reduced orders; FY28-29 assume normal monsoons, new plants for the parent and steady launches (+10% and +9%). The EBITDA margin stays around 20-20.5%, management's floor. Interest income follows the cash pile at 7.5-8.5%. Every assumption is in the Excel model's Assumptions sheet, which recalculates this report's target price.

blocks.callout: We are ~12% below the street for FY28 mainly on revenue: brokers assume ~20% growth in FY28 after a flat FY27 (ICICI Securities models 12% a year from FY26). Sumitomo India has not grown revenue since FY23, and management's 12-14% aspiration was not repeated in 2026. If the parent's plants and molecules do deliver, the bull case covers it.

sections.title: The street: few analysts, all positive, and slow to cut

blocks.p: Coverage is thin. Only three houses have notes we could open: ICICI Securities (institutional), ICICI Direct (its retail arm) and Anand Rathi, all with BUY ratings. Of nine analysts polled by S&P, six say Strong Buy, two Buy and one Hold, with an average target of ~₹584, but most targets were set in May-July 2026, before the monsoon failed and Q2 disappointed. ICICI Securities cut its target to ₹485 on 28-Oct-2026. The bull case on the street rests on the parent: its molecules, its plants in India and, since July, its semiconductor-chemicals plans.

blocks.h: How the street values Sumitomo Chemical

blocks.p: Every broker whose method we could find values SCIL on **P/E on FY28E earnings**: ICICI Direct 45x, Anand Rathi 40x (raised from 36x for the semiconductor option), ICICI Securities 36.5x (averaged with 29x EV/EBITDA). We use the same method so that our target is comparable, applied to the earnings the market will look at in October 2027 (Sep-28E: half FY28E, half FY29E). The gap between us and the street is in the multiple and in our lower earnings, not in the method.

blocks.callout: **What the cross-checks tell us.** EV/EBITDA (18x Sep-28E EBITDA plus the cash at face value) gives ₹340, 7% below the P/E target: the difference is the premium a P/E puts on interest income. The DCF (₹232) is far lower: at an 11.6% cost of capital, ~20% EBITDA margins and our growth, cash flows support well under today's price. The market has always priced SCIL for faster growth than it has delivered; if growth stays at high single digits, the multiple has further to fall.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good franchise, but the growth has to come back first

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** one of India's widest crop-protection distribution networks, exclusive access to a global innovator's patented molecules, ~20% EBITDA margins, disciplined dealer credit and ₹2,500 cr of cash with no debt.

**What you are paying:** 27.2x our FY28E earnings for a company whose revenue has not grown in three years, whose best new idea may sit with its parent, and whose cash earns 7%. On the street's method and our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): fair, not cheap. Cash-adjusted cross-checks are lower.

bullets: **Rating: HOLD, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).** Our ratings: BUY above 15% expected return, SELL below −10%.
**Buy below ~₹315**, or on proof that domestic revenue is growing at double digits again.
**Sell above ~₹405**, or if the monsoon fails again in 2027.
**Biggest swing factor:** the monsoon. One season decides the year; two weak ones in a row would test the 28x multiple.

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Insecticides, herbicides (weedkillers), fungicides and other chemicals that protect crops.
A molecule whose patent has expired; many companies can make it, so it competes on price.
A newer product still protected by patent or data rights; here mostly from the parent, Sumitomo Chemical Japan.
Technical = the pure active ingredient; formulation = the product mixed for farmers to spray.
India's monsoon (June-October) and winter (November-March) cropping seasons.
Plant growth regulator: products that change how a plant grows or ripens (e.g. gibberellic acid).
Fumigants (e.g. aluminium phosphide) used to protect stored grain.
Products based on natural organisms or extracts that protect or strengthen crops.
Making a specific molecule for another company (here, the parent) under contract.
Discounts and incentives paid to distributors and dealers, deducted from revenue.
Indian rule that at least 25% of a listed company's shares must be held by the public; caps the promoter at 75%.
Share price ÷ earnings per share; enterprise value (market value less net cash) ÷ operating profit before depreciation.
Discounted cash flow valuation; WACC is the required annual return used to discount future cash.
